catalog_quote: [BHT 1976 p.185] Like most other Bantu languages, Haya, a language of Northern Tanzania, is characterized by two level tones, H (high) and L (low) ... In section 2 we argue that these alternations can only be understood in terms of an abstract phrase-penultimate accent. [p.191] Many Bantu languages have a phrase-penultimate accent which usually lengthens the vowel of that syllable, and perhaps has some additional pitch and intensity effects. If we look at a Haya word such as [okugulu] 'leg', with all L tones, we note neither a lengthening of the penultimate vowel, nor any pitch perturbation suggesting an accent on that (or any other) syllable. [p.194] Haya assigns a phrase-penultimate accent by means of the rule in (24). (24) Syl → [+accent] / ___ Syl % The second syllable preceding the % boundary receives an accent whose only effect is tonal (namely, rules (4') and (6')). [p.195] Unlike other Bantu tone languages such as Shona, Tswana, etc., there is no accentual feature which we can single out as evidence for the penultimate accent. [Hyman & Byarushengo 1984 p.88] Instead, it has anticipation conditioned by the % boundary in (66), a property characteristic of accent (cf. Becker 1978; Hyman 1978). We leave open the possibility that the final two syllables before a % boundary constitute a foot.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Haya (haya1250) is not in the catalog. Both title-keyword items were run down. (1) Byarushengo, Hyman & Tenenbaum 1976 'Tone, accent, and assertion in Haya' was OBTAINED: Hyman's Berkeley CV gives a USC GSIL URL for the whole SCOPIL 3 volume (image-only scan, 152 MB); it was downloaded to and pp. 185-206 were scanned (one tesseract at a time, 300 dpi) into bht1976_ocr/. The paper states that Haya has two tones H/L, no phonetic stress (no penultimate lengthening or pitch perturbation on all-L words, p. 191; 'no accentual feature which we can single out', p. 195), and only an abstract phrase-penultimate accent before the % boundary realised as H-L -> F-L and L-H -> H-H, plus H-lowering next to pause. This is the best first-hand statement for a stress catalog: tone language, no word stress, phrase-level penultimate tonal accent. The same CV URL pattern yielded SCOPIL 6 'Haya grammatical structure' (1977; 111 MB, saved), whose 'Preliminaries' sect. 2.3 (p. 5, scanned in scopil6_prelim_ocr/) restates the analysis; this closes the 'the named source could not be reached' classification recorded for that volume in (2) Philippson 1991/92 thesis 'Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale' (Paris 5, 542 pp.): theses.fr record says not accessible online; no HAL deposit, no Google Books or open copy found; only the abstract was read (typology of ~30 East African Bantu languages from full tone to penultimate demarcative stress). Whether it treats Haya is unverified; priority medium, print only. Also re-read from the earlier reading: Hyman & Byarushengo 1984 (Google preview, p. 88 conclusion: accent-like properties, possible final foot before %), Rehse 1912 pp. 4-5 and Herrmann 1904 p. 151 (colonial 'Betonung' remarks = tone marking, superseded). Hyman 2007/2009/2017 PhonLab papers held by the project cite Haya as a non-culminative /H, Ø/ tone system with penultimate L% attraction, consistent with BHT.fr, HAL, Crossref, Google Books API, USC GSIL); in the haya1250 folder was appended with every new file.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Haya is a tone language (privative /H/ vs. toneless, default L); there is no lexical word stress. The only positional prominence effects are phrasal: at the end of an assertion phrase (%), a penultimate H becomes a HL fall and a final H is anticipated onto the penult, after which any H immediately before pause is lowered (and an utterance-initial augment H is lowered after pause). The authors treat these as accent-like properties of an otherwise tonal system and explicitly leave open a phrase-final disyllabic foot; Hyman (2007:674, open PhonLab report, saved) later states outright that 'Haya has a full tone system whose Hs are not obligatory, culminative, or metrical', and Hyman (2009:195) summarizes the 1976 analysis as a phrase-final L% 'drawn to the penult'. Haya is not reported to have Bantu-style penultimate lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; no metrical structure posited at word level.
new_statements.exceptions: The HL/anticipation rules are keyed to the % (assertion-final) boundary, not to pause: vocative-preceding nouns (omútí káto) undergo them without being prepausal; negative and 'marked' TAMs and nouns before possessives/adjectives undergo H-tone reduction instead (pp.57, 73, 78). LH rising tones created by very late rules (h-deletion, mu -> syllabic m) escape contour simplification (p.88).
new_statements.domain_note: Phrase/utterance level (end of assertion, pre-pausal), realized on the penultimate and final syllables of the phrase; citation forms of nouns therefore show at most one H or HL (e.g. o-mú-ti 'tree' from /ó-mu-tí/), which the authors warn is misleading about the word-level system (p.56 per snippet; Hyman 2007:665). Data represent E. R. Byarushengo's Haya (Bukoba area); dialect footnote (p.54 n.1) not visible in preview.
new_statements.identity_note: Hyman & Byarushengo 1984 describe the Haya of co-author E. R. Byarushengo (Bukoba area, Tanzania); the dialect footnote (p.54 n.1) was not visible in the preview. The two colonial-era sketches describe named varieties: Rehse 1912/13 describes 'Ruziba', the speech of Kiziba (the Ziba/Kiziba dialect of Haya), and Herrmann 1904 describes 'Lusiba', specifically the 'Bayossa' dialect of Kjamtwara (Kyamutwara), both within Glottolog haya1250. Both old sketches use 'Betonung/Ton' impressionistically for what modern work analyses as H tone (Rehse: position depends only on grammatical form, no rule statable; Herrmann: penult, antepenult or pre-antepenult, variable even within one speaker's sentence).

new_statements.quote: Many Bantu languages have a phrase-penultimate accent which usually lengthens the vowel of that syllable, and perhaps has some additional pitch and intensity effects. If we look at a Haya word such as [okugulu] 'leg', with all L tones, we note neither a lengthening of the penultimate vowel, nor any pitch perturbation suggesting an accent on that (or any other) syllable. However, both rule (4) and rule (6) have the effect of bringing more prominence to the penultimate syllable. Rule (4), it is recalled, changes a H to a F tone when it is in penultimate position. Rule (6) has the effect of transferring a H from final to penultimate position.

new_statements.reading: Haya is a two-tone (H/L) Bantu language with no phonetic word stress: an all-low word shows no penultimate lengthening and no pitch prominence on any syllable, and the authors say outright (p. 195) that there is no accentual feature they can single out. The only 'accent' is an abstract phrase-penultimate accent, assigned to the second syllable before the phrase boundary % (not the word), whose sole exponents are tonal: H-L becomes falling-L and L-H becomes H-H before %, and H is lowered adjacent to pause. For a word-stress catalog this reads as: tone language, no word-level stress; phrase-level penultimate tonal accent only. Byarushengo 1977 (Preliminaries, p. 5) restates the same analysis; Hyman & Byarushengo 1984 (p. 88) keeps it and leaves open a final bisyllabic foot before %. The 1904 and 1912 German 'Betonung' remarks (Herrmann: penult/antepenult, freely variable; Rehse: depends only on grammatical form) are impressionistic tone-marking and are superseded.

new_statements.quote: [p.117] In addition, some of us have been so sensitive, perhaps in vain, to the struggle to establish criteria for tone vs. accent that we have contradicted ourselves — I for example argued originally for accent in Haya, then tone; ... The penultimate cases are relatively non-controversial and may have a number of surface manifestations, as summarized in (5). (5) a. stress, e.g., Swahili b. vowel-lengthening, e.g., Southern Bantu (Doke 1967) c. attraction of H tone, e.g., Chizigula [p.118] Other Bantu languages show attraction to a metrically strong position. The nature of this attraction can be LINKING, SHIFTING, or SPREADING of a tone (usually H, but also potentially L, as in Haya (Byarushengo, Hyman and Tenenbaum 1976)).

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with both existing statements (Byarushengo, Hyman & Tenenbaum 1976; Hyman & Byarushengo 1984): Haya is a two-tone language with no phonetic word stress and only an abstract phrase-penultimate tonal accent that attracts/adjusts tones. The 1989 appraisal adds the author's own retrospective that the 'accent' analysis of Haya was abandoned in favour of a purely tonal one, and it does not restate the p.191/p.195 observation of 1976 (no lengthening, no pitch prominence) in its own words; the tonal-attraction characterization is the deciding statement. It does not contradict anything in the catalog.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Haya is treated as a tone language. The only 'accent' the paper attributes to it is the tonal-attraction kind of (5c): a metrically strong (phrase-)penultimate position that attracts a tone, in Haya an L tone (the H-L > falling-L / L-H > H-H adjustments before the phrase boundary described in Byarushengo, Hyman & Tenenbaum 1976). No stress, vowel lengthening or other phonetic prominence is claimed for any Haya syllable, and Hyman states that he gave up his earlier accentual analysis of Haya for a tonal one. The conclusion (p. 129) says such Bantu accents exist for the sole purpose of placing tones and have no segmental correlate.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Haya. pp. 127-128 add only that in Haya a second object prefix brings its own H tone and that the suffixal H may be an enclitic or separate phonological word (citing Hyman 1989, The consequences of rule ordering in Haya tonology); these are tonal, not stress, remarks.
new_statements.identity_note: Hyman 1989 names no Haya dialect; its Haya data come from the Byarushengo/Hyman work (Byarushengo's own speech). The older German sources held by the project describe particular dialects (Rehse 1912 = Kiziba/Ruziba; Herrmann 1904 = Bayossa of Kyamtwara). Philippson 1992 (not opened) is an East African Bantu survey and its abstract does not name Haya.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (classification tonal; BHT 1976: two level tones, no penultimate lengthening or pitch prominence on an all-L word, only an abstract phrase-penultimate accent with tonal exponents) and with Hyman & Byarushengo 1984 (H-L -> HL-L and L-H -> H-H before the phrase boundary, final H lowered before pause): Philippson restates exactly these pre-pausal rules (p.325, p.484-485, annex item 9) and adds an explicit typological placement: Haya's penultimate has no culmination of pitch, length or intensity (type d, p.484), in contrast with its group-III relatives Nyoro/Tooro, which have lost distinctive tone and have a demarcative penultimate accent (annex p.499, p.486).…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Haya (Rutara, Philippson's group III) is for Philippson a 'langue accentuelle à mélodie H', i.e. a restricted tone / tonal-accent system: a stem carries at most one lexically marked ('accented') syllable and the only melody is a H tone that associates to it, all other syllables getting L by default (disyllabic noun stems show exactly three patterns: no accent emfulu, accent on stem-initial enjóka, accent on stem-final empunú; vowel length is contrastive). This 'accent' is a diacritic for H placement, not stress. On word/phrase prominence he is explicit: in his typology of the penultimate (§3.5.2) Haya is NOT among the languages with a culmination of pitch, length or intensity on the penult (types a-c, e.g. Nyoro/Tooro with a demarcative penultimate accent) but in type (d), 'languages whose penultimate is not marked by any of these parameters' and whose penult matters only as a limit for tonal association: before pause / certain syntactic boundaries a final H is copied/retracted onto the penult and dissociated from the final before absolute pause, and a penultimate H followed by L is realized falling (p.325, p.484-485, annex item 9-10). So: tone (tonal-accent) language, no word stress; only phrase-final (pre-pausal) tonal effects on the penult, as in Byarushengo, Hyman & Tenenbaum 1976.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none: no secondary stress or rhythmic prominence is described for Haya; p.326 n.1 only remarks that the restriction of the pre-pausal modulation rule to final and penultimate position 'laisse supposer une analyse métrique en pieds binaires; je ne la poursuivrai pas ici'.
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal-accent particulars, not stress: nominals have at most one accent per stem and the augment is always accented (p.319); a head noun loses its accent before a directly governed augmentless modifier except numerals, demonstratives and the possessives -aaNge 'my' / -aawe 'your', which instead add an accent on the noun's final syllable (pp.319-322); verbs may carry several H and are realized all-L before a direct complement (p.323); Meeussen's rule is active (p.321); in Nyambo the HL/LH stem contrast is neutralized and in Kerebe and some Nyankore-Kiga subdialects the -cvcv́ pattern merged with -cvcv (p.188); diachronically Haya is placed at 'stade III' (tonal system reduced to an accentual one under Meeussen's rule, p.487), short of the stages IV-V where a metrical/demarcative penultimate accent emerges.
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's Haya is (Ru)Haya of Bukoba, group III 'Rutara' with Nyambo, Zinza, Kerebe, Nyankore/Kiga, Nyoro/Tooro; his Haya data follow Byarushengo, Hyman & Tenenbaum 1976 / Hyman & Byarushengo 1984 (cited pp.19, 21) plus his own Tanzanian survey material; Nyambo (treated separately, annex p.500) and Kerebe are noted as differing in the -cvcv́ pattern (p.188).

tone_statements.quote: 慣用的正書法ではアクセント表記をすることはないが，ここでは，高く発音される母音や子音前鼻音の上に´をつけて，低く発音されるそれらから区別する。...子音(+y/w)をC，母音をV，子音前鼻音をNであらわし，また，長母音の後半部分または母音につづく母音とNをRであらわす。アクセント表記を伴う場合は，V́，Ń，Ŕで高いV，N，Rをあらわし，低いそれらと区別する。... [p.85] この言語の動詞は，アクセントの面で2つに分類しうる。そして，その区別は不定形においても明確にあらわれる。その第一の型（A型と呼ぶことにする）には，たとえば次のようなものが属する。okúlya「食べる」, okubóna「見る」... これらのアクセントは，okuCV́X で表示することができる。
tone_statements.translation: The customary orthography does not mark accent, but here an acute ´ is placed over vowels and preconsonantal nasals pronounced high, to distinguish them from those pronounced low. ... A consonant (+y/w) is written C, a vowel V, a preconsonantal nasal N, and the second half of a long vowel, or a vowel or N following a vowel, R. With accent marking, V́, Ń, Ŕ stand for high V, N, R, distinguished from low ones. ... [p.85] The verbs of this language can be divided into two classes with respect to accent, and the distinction appears clearly in the infinitive too. To the first type (call it type A) belong e.g. okúlya 'eat', okubóna 'see' ... Their accent can be represented as okuCV́X.

tone_statements.quote: we shall argue that Haya (and many other closely related languages) is a version of Voorhoeve’s restricted tone system in two senses. First, we shall argue that underlying forms are incompletely specified for tone ... Second, the underlying tone which is indicated is restricted to H only. ... The following generalizations characterize the surface tone patterns in (1): (i) There are primarily two tones, H and L. (ii) There is no rising tone, and the observed falling tone can occur only in penultimate position (i.e. as -V̂CV or -V́VCV). (iii) H tone never appears immediately before pause

tone_statements.summary: Two surface tones H/L, HL fall only phrase-penultimate; underlying H vs. toneless, at most one H per morpheme, L by default rule; earlier called 'tonal accent' by the authors. Forms: at least 60.

sources.note: Haya analysed as a restricted tone system (underlying H vs. zero, L filled in by default); earlier 'tonal accent' analysis abandoned (p.54). Surface falling tone only in penultimate position (p.55); before the % phrase boundary (end of assertion) H-L -> HL-L and L-H -> H-H, then any pre-pausal H is lowered and a post-pausal initial-vowel H is lowered (p.57); H anticipation before % is 'a property characteristic of accent'; authors 'leave open the possibility that the final two syllables before a % boundary constitute a foot' (p.88). No word-stress rule stated.

tone.quote: we shall argue that Haya (and many other closely related languages) is a version of Voorhoeve’s restricted tone system in two senses. First, we shall argue that underlying forms are incompletely specified for tone ... Second, the underlying tone which is indicated is restricted to H only. ... The following generalizations characterize the surface tone patterns in (1): (i) There are primarily two tones, H and L. (ii) There is no rising tone, and the observed falling tone can occur only in penultimate position (i.e. as -V̂CV or -V́VCV). (iii) H tone never appears immediately before pause

tone.summary: Two surface tones H/L, HL fall only phrase-penultimate; underlying H vs. toneless, at most one H per morpheme, L by default rule; earlier called 'tonal accent' by the authors. Forms: at least 60.
tone.says: Two surface tones H/L, HL fall only phrase-penultimate; underlying H vs. toneless, at most one H per morpheme, L by default rule; earlier called 'tonal accent' by the authors. Forms: at least 60.

sources.citation: Byarushengo, Ernest Rugwa, Larry M. Hyman & Sarah Tenenbaum. 1976. Tone, accent, and assertion in Haya. In Larry M. Hyman (ed.), Studies in Bantu tonology (SCOPIL 3), 185-205. Los Angeles: Dept. of Linguistics, USC.
sources.quote: Many Bantu languages have a phrase-penultimate accent which usually lengthens the vowel of that syllable, and perhaps has some additional pitch and intensity effects. If we look at a Haya word such as [okugulu] 'leg', with all L tones, we note neither a lengthening of the penultimate vowel, nor any pitch perturbation suggesting an accent on that (or any other) syllable. However, both rule (4) and rule (6) have the effect of bringing more prominence to the penultimate syllable. Rule (4), it is recalled, changes a H to a F tone when it is in penultimate position. Rule (6) has the effect of transferring a H from final to penultimate position. (p. 191)
sources.locator: p. 185 (sect. 0), pp. 187-190 (rules 4, 6, table 16), p. 191 (sect. 2 ACCENT), p. 195, p. 203 (conclusion), p. 204 n. 9
sources.note: Haya has two level tones H and L (p. 185); there is no phonetic word stress: an all-L word shows no penultimate lengthening and no pitch perturbation on any syllable (p. 191), and 'there is no accentual feature which we can single out as evidence for the penultimate accent' (p. 195). The authors nevertheless posit an ABSTRACT phrase-penultimate accent, assigned to the second syllable before the phrase boundary % (rule 24, p. 194-195), whose only exponents are tonal: underlying H-L becomes F-L and L-H becomes H-H immediately before %; H is lowered next to pause (pp. 187-191, table 16 p. 190).…

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. [...] Une trentaine de langues en tout sont utilisées comme exemples. Enfin, on établit systématiquement les correspondances prosodiques entre chacune des langues concernées et le bantu commun et on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernés a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale.

sources.quote: [p.117] In addition, some of us have been so sensitive, perhaps in vain, to the struggle to establish criteria for tone vs. accent that we have contradicted ourselves — I for example argued originally for accent in Haya, then tone; ... The penultimate cases are relatively non-controversial and may have a number of surface manifestations, as summarized in (5). (5) a. stress, e.g., Swahili b. vowel-lengthening, e.g., Southern Bantu (Doke 1967) c. attraction of H tone, e.g., Chizigula [p.118] Other Bantu languages show attraction to a metrically strong position. tone.translation: The customary orthography does not mark accent, but here an acute ´ is placed over vowels and preconsonantal nasals pronounced high, to distinguish them from those pronounced low. ... A consonant (+y/w) is written C, a vowel V, a preconsonantal nasal N, and the second half of a long vowel, or a vowel or N following a vowel, R. With accent marking, V́, Ń, Ŕ stand for high V, N, R, distinguished from low ones. ... [p.85] The verbs of this language can be divided into two classes with respect to accent, and the distinction appears clearly in the infinitive too. To the first type (call it type A) belong e.g. okúlya 'eat', okubóna 'see' ... Their accent can be represented as okuCV́X.
